Prised
PRYZD
v. (past participle; priced, valued, appraised at a sum)
From Old French prisier, to value, from Latin pretium, price. Prise in older English means to set a price on, to appraise; prize in the sense of esteeming highly is the same root. The Hebrew yaqar means to be valued or esteemed.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The shepherd-prophet of Zechariah 11, rejected by the flock he fed, asks for his wages and is paid thirty pieces of silver. God's answer is bitter irony: “And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD” (Zechariah 11:13). To be prised is to be priced, appraised at a sum. The sum was the compensation for a dead slave under the law of Exodus 21, and the speaker is the LORD Himself in the person of His shepherd: this is what Israel reckoned Him worth. The whole transaction had been set up two verses earlier: “So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver” (Zechariah 11:12). Five centuries later Matthew records the fulfilment to the coin, the man, the sum and the destination: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value” (Matthew 27:9). Judas, the priests, the potter's field: every detail of the prophecy came in.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): PRISE, to set a price on; to value; to appraise; PRISED, valued; appraised.

expand to see more

PRISE or PRIZE, v.t. To set or estimate the value of; to rate; to appraise.

To value highly; to esteem; to regard as of great worth.

PRISED, pp. Rated; valued; appraised.

From Latin pretium, a price, through Old French prisier.

Zechariah 11:13 says, a goodly price that I was prised at of them.

Key Scripture

Zec 11:13 — "And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD."

Zec 11:12 — "And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver."

Mat 27:9 — "Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value;"

Modern Corruption

The thirty pieces are explained as a detail Matthew read backwards into Zechariah, denying genuine predictive prophecy and the sovereignty that governed the betrayal.

expand to see more

The standard critical account runs thus: the Gospel writers searched the prophets for texts that could be bent to fit events, and Matthew's citation here — which names Jeremy where the words stand in Zechariah — proves the method was careless. On that reading there is no prophecy, only retrofitting. The dictionary rejects the premise. Scripture declares the end from the beginning, and Matthew's composite citation follows a recognised Jewish convention of naming the greater prophet in whose roll the collection stood, with Jeremiah's own potter and field in view.

What the critical reading destroys is the doctrine of the two causes in the betrayal. Judas sold freely and is guilty; the price, the field and the potter were determined before Judas was born. Peter preaches both at Pentecost: delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and by wicked hands crucified and slain. The thirty pieces of silver are the hinge of that doctrine, and the prophecy insists upon it with heavy irony — a goodly price.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French prisier, from Latin pretium, a price; Zechariah 11:13 has the LORD prised at thirty pieces of silver.

expand to see more

Latin pretium, a price, through Old French prisier, to value.

Hebrew yaqar, to be valued or esteemed.

Zechariah 11:13 is the only occurrence of prised in the Authorized Version.

Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation for a dead slave (Exodus 21:32).

Matthew 27:9 records the fulfilment to the sum and the potter's field.
